A ridiculous FOUNTAIN of colourful soft balls blasts upward from the crocodile’s mouth and rains across the garden.

Dozens of balls bounce everywhere.

Luca tries to dodge them but becomes surrounded up to his shoulders.

At the final moment, only Luca’s shocked face is visible between bouncing colourful balls.

HARD CUT while balls are still falling.

No fade-out.

--------------------------------------------------
MOTION / RETENTION RULES
--------------------------------------------------
- Something physical must happen every 1–2 seconds.
- Luca must actively catch, throw, dodge, step back, roll, and react.
- Do NOT make Luca stand still watching for long periods.
- Do NOT add a second absurd rule.
- Do NOT grow or shrink the crocodile.
- Do NOT grow or shrink Luca.
- Do NOT transform the garden.
- Only the NUMBER OF BALLS increases.
- The escalation must feel obvious: 1 ball → 3 balls → 6 balls → huge final fountain.
- Ball motion must be large and easy to read on a phone screen.
- Keep the crocodile friendly and funny.
- No dangerous contact with Luca.
- No biting.
- No sharp attack behavior.

--------------------------------------------------
AUDIO / SOUND DESIGN
--------------------------------------------------
No dialogue.
No narrator.
No lip-sync.

Use clear comedy sound effects:
- soft GULP for balls entering
- playful PTOO for balls exiting
- light BOING sounds when balls bounce
- one comic HIC before the final fountain

Background music:
Fast playful absurd preschool comedy, around 118 BPM.
Pizzicato strings + marimba + soft percussion.
Music builds slightly with each multiplication step.
Brief near-silence before the final fountain.
No vocals.

--------------------------------------------------
NEGATIVE / DO NOT GENERATE
--------------------------------------------------
NO text overlay.
NO subtitles.
NO logo.
NO captions.
NO pond.
NO water.
NO extra children.
NO scary crocodile behavior.
NO biting.
NO chasing.
NO camera spin.
NO scene change.
NO random objects.
NO body deformation.
NO extra limbs.
NO character redesign.

DO NOT redesign Luca.
DO NOT redesign the crocodile.
DO NOT replace the scene.
DO NOT add a pond.
DO NOT change the balls to only red balls.
DO NOT add extra characters.

SERIES TONE:
Absurd Moments.
Fast, visual, silly physical comedy.
No educational dialogue.
The joke must work with sound OFF.

CORE ABSURD RULE:
Every time a ball goes into the crocodile’s mouth, it spits back MORE balls than it received.

IMPORTANT:
The crocodile is a silly toy-like character, not a predator.
It NEVER bites, chases, threatens, or attacks Luca.
The balls are soft lightweight play balls.
The crocodile behaves like a ridiculous living ball machine.

CAMERA:
One continuous shot.
Stable camera.
No camera rotation.
No cutaways.
No establishing shot.
Keep Luca and the crocodile readable in the same frame whenever possible.
Do not zoom excessively.
Do not change location.

--------------------------------------------------
0.0–0.8 SEC — FIRST-FRAME HOOK
--------------------------------------------------
START EXACTLY FROM THE PROVIDED IMAGE.

Luca is already recoiling in surprise.
The crocodile’s huge open mouth is already full of colourful soft balls.

Immediately:
PTOO!

ONE colourful ball shoots out of the crocodile’s mouth toward Luca.

Luca flinches and catches/blocks it with both hands.

No pause.

--------------------------------------------------
0.8–3.5 SEC — FIRST ACTION
--------------------------------------------------
Luca quickly tosses that ONE ball back into the crocodile’s open mouth.

GULP.

The crocodile freezes for half a beat.
Its cheeks puff slightly.

PTOO-PTOO-PTOO!

It spits out THREE colourful balls in quick succession.

Luca dodges one, catches one, and one bounces off the grass beside him.

Keep the action fast and readable.

--------------------------------------------------
3.5–6.5 SEC — ESCALATION
--------------------------------------------------
Luca grabs TWO nearby balls and throws BOTH back into the crocodile’s mouth.

GULP-GULP.

The crocodile’s cheeks puff much bigger.

For one short beat, everything is silent.

Then:

PTOO-PTOO-PTOO-PTOO-PTOO-PTOO!

A burst of SIX soft balls fires out rapidly.

Luca jumps backward while balls bounce around his feet.

--------------------------------------------------
6.5–9.5 SEC — LUCA TRIES TO STOP IT
--------------------------------------------------
Luca raises both hands as if saying “enough.”

He carefully picks up only ONE ball.

He slowly rolls it toward the crocodile instead of throwing it.

The crocodile gently catches it.

GULP.

Luca waits nervously.

--------------------------------------------------
9.5–11.5 SEC — FAKE RESOLUTION
--------------------------------------------------
The crocodile returns exactly ONE ball.

PTOO.

Luca catches it.

Both Luca and the crocodile relax.

The crocodile closes its mouth and smiles innocently.

Luca smiles with relief.

Hold this calm moment for LESS THAN ONE SECOND.

--------------------------------------------------
11.5–15.0 SEC — HUGE FINAL TWIST
--------------------------------------------------
The crocodile suddenly gets a strange hiccup.

HIC!

Its cheeks inflate enormously.

Luca’s smile disappears.

Then:

PTOO-PTOO-PTOO-PTOO-PTOO!

A ridiculous FOUNTAIN of colourful soft balls blasts upward from the crocodile’s mouth and rains across the garden.

Dozens of balls bounce everywhere.

Luca tries to dodge them but becomes surrounded up to his shoulders.

At the final moment, only Luca’s shocked face is visible between bouncing colourful balls.

HARD CUT while balls are still falling.

No fade-out.

--------------------------------------------------
MOTION / RETENTION RULES
--------------------------------------------------
- Something physical must happen every 1–2 seconds.
- Luca must actively catch, throw, dodge, step back, roll, and react.
- Do NOT make Luca stand still watching for long periods.
- Do NOT add a second absurd rule.
- Do NOT grow or shrink the crocodile.
- Do NOT grow or shrink Luca.
- Do NOT transform the garden.
- Only the NUMBER OF BALLS increases.
- The escalation must feel obvious: 1 ball → 3 balls → 6 balls → huge final fountain.
- Ball motion must be large and easy to read on a phone screen.
- Keep the crocodile friendly and funny.
- No dangerous contact with Luca.
- No biting.
- No sharp attack behavior.

--------------------------------------------------
AUDIO / SOUND DESIGN
--------------------------------------------------
No dialogue.
No narrator.
No lip-sync.

Use clear comedy sound effects:
- soft GULP for balls entering
- playful PTOO for balls exiting
- light BOING sounds when balls bounce
- one comic HIC before the final fountain

Background music:
Fast playful absurd preschool comedy, around 118 BPM.
Pizzicato strings + marimba + soft percussion.
Music builds slightly with each multiplication step.
Brief near-silence before the final fountain.
No vocals.

--------------------------------------------------
NEGATIVE / DO NOT GENERATE
--------------------------------------------------
NO text overlay.
NO subtitles.
NO logo.
NO captions.
NO pond.
NO water.
NO extra children.
NO scary crocodile behavior.
NO biting.
NO chasing.
NO camera spin.
NO scene change.
NO random objects.
NO body deformation.
NO extra limbs.
NO character redesign.

beats.sourceQuote:
11.5–15.0 SEC — HUGE FINAL TWIST
--------------------------------------------------
The crocodile suddenly gets a strange hiccup.

HIC!

Its cheeks inflate enormously.

Luca’s smile disappears.

Then:

PTOO-PTOO-PTOO-PTOO-PTOO!

A ridiculous FOUNTAIN of colourful soft balls blasts upward from the crocodile’s mouth and rains across the garden.

Dozens of balls bounce everywhere.

Luca tries to dodge them but becomes surrounded up to his shoulders.

At the final moment, only Luca’s shocked face is visible between bouncing colourful balls.

HARD CUT while balls are still falling.

No fade-out.

--------------------------------------------------
MOTION / RETENTION RULES
--------------------------------------------------
- Something physical must happen every 1–2 seconds.
- Luca must actively catch, throw, dodge, step back, roll, and react.
- Do NOT make Luca stand still watching for long periods.
- Do NOT add a second absurd rule.
- Do NOT grow or shrink the crocodile.
- Do NOT grow or shrink Luca.
- Do NOT transform the garden.
- Only the NUMBER OF BALLS increases.
- The escalation must feel obvious: 1 ball → 3 balls → 6 balls → huge final fountain.
- Ball motion must be large and easy to read on a phone screen.
- Keep the crocodile friendly and funny.
- No dangerous contact with Luca.
- No biting.
- No sharp attack behavior.

--------------------------------------------------
AUDIO / SOUND DESIGN
--------------------------------------------------
No dialogue.
No narrator.
No lip-sync.

Use clear comedy sound effects:
- soft GULP for balls entering
- playful PTOO for balls exiting
- light BOING sounds when balls bounce
- one comic HIC before the final fountain

Background music:
Fast playful absurd preschool comedy, around 118 BPM.
Pizzicato strings + marimba + soft percussion.
Music builds slightly with each multiplication step.
Brief near-silence before the final fountain.
No vocals.

--------------------------------------------------
NEGATIVE / DO NOT GENERATE
--------------------------------------------------
NO text overlay.
NO subtitles.
NO logo.
NO captions.
NO pond.
NO water.
NO extra children.
NO scary crocodile behavior.
NO biting.
NO chasing.
NO camera spin.
NO scene change.
NO random objects.
NO body deformation.
NO extra limbs.
NO character redesign.

engineInput.prompt:
# Luca vs Box Cat — OpenArt / Seedance 2.0 Mini

## Core concept
Luca wants to use an empty toy box.

**Single animal rule:** whenever the box becomes empty and usable, the cat claims it again.

## Prompt
Colorful high-quality stylized 3D preschool animation in the official Pompom Hills style. 9:16 vertical, 15 seconds, one continuous fixed-camera shot in a warm simple playroom. Keep Luca, one rigid toy box and one stylized cat clearly visible. No cuts, no zoom, no shake.

Use the official Luca design exactly: messy dark brown hair, green/cream mountain shirt, green shorts, orange sneakers. Use one cute stylized cat with a simple smooth coat, low-detail fur, calm expression.

### Frame zero — conflict already happening
Start with Luca already reaching toward the toy box, but the cat is already curled up inside it. Luca's hand is paused just above the rim and he is looking at the cat.

### Attempt 1 — clear the box
Luca gently gestures the cat out of the box without touching it. The cat steps out. Luca turns back toward the box. The cat calmly steps back inside before Luca can use it. Luca gives a tiny puzzled look.

### Attempt 2 — move the box
Luca lifts the rigid empty box, moves it a short distance, and sets it down. He turns his head away for a brief moment. When he looks back, the cat is already sitting inside again.

### Attempt 3 — guard the box
Luca stays beside the empty box and watches carefully. The cat waits nearby. Luca looks away for just a moment toward the shelf. When he looks back, the cat has claimed the box again.

### Fake win + final payoff
The cat finally stays a short distance away. Luca sees the empty box and gives a small confident smile. He bends toward it to use it. Just before his hands reach the box, the cat makes one short calm move into the box and curls up again. Luca's hands stop in the air. Cat looks completely comfortable. Hard cut.

## Performance
Luca stays energetic, confident and determined. Cat stays calm and innocent. Comedy comes from Luca's serious effort versus the cat's complete certainty that the box belongs to it.

## Guardrails
- one Luca only
- one cat only
- one rigid toy box only
- same rule throughout: EMPTY BOX -> CAT CLAIMS BOX
- no chasing
- no jumping onto Luca
- no complex cat acrobatics
- no child-cat body contact
- no realistic fur simulation
- fixed camera
- one continuous take
- hard cut on Luca's frozen hands

engineInput.prompt:
Create a premium 23-26 second vertical 9:16 Pompom Hills Instagram Reel.

MAIN CHARACTER:
LUCA - official reference exactly.

GUEST:
Friendly castaway explorer inspired by classic public-domain shipwreck adventure literature. Simple weathered clothes, handmade satchel, coconut in hand. No modern film likeness.

SETTING:
Bright tropical dream island.

0.0-1.2 SEC - HOOK
Luca lies on soft sand. A wave splashes nearby. A tropical bird calls loudly.
Luca bolts upright.
Luca: "WHERE AM I?!"
Guest steps in holding a coconut.
Guest: "An island."

1.2-5.0 SEC
Luca looks around: palm trees, bright sea, map sticking from pocket.
Luca: "Adventure!"
Guest: "First... survival."

5.0-10.0 SEC - COMEDY MONTAGE
Luca tries opening a coconut. It rolls away.
He tries fishing. Fish steals the bait.
He builds a shelter. One leaf falls onto his head.
Luca: "I'm usually GOOD at exploring!"
Guest laughs: "Different island."

10.0-16.0 SEC
They find a small cave. Inside: an old wooden chest.
Luca: "TREASURE!"
He opens it.
Inside: a blank journal and pencil.
Luca: "A notebook?"
Guest: "Every adventure needs a story."

16.0-21.5 SEC
Luca writes and draws on the beach.
Luca: "Today... I became an island explorer."
Wind turns a page.

21.5-25.5 SEC - TWIST
SMASH CUT: Luca wakes in his own bed.
Luca: "A dream?"
Then notices the SAME journal in his hand.
He stares at camera.
CUT.

No narration. No on-screen text.

details.recommendation:
Before writing a 15-second prompt, verify that the core mechanic
can naturally generate at least 4 visually distinct consequences.

If it cannot, reject the concept.

Do NOT stretch a two-beat teaching contrast into 15 seconds.

evaluations.message: Only 1 distinct visual consequences detected. Minimum: 4. Core mechanic insufficient for 15 seconds.

details.recommendation:
No single visual state may occupy more than approximately
25–30% of the entire video unless meaningful new physical
consequences occur within that state.

Different dialogue or tiny movements do NOT count
as different visual beats.

evaluations.message: Good visual state distribution. Max state: 11.5%.

details.recommendation:
The same physical action should not repeat more than twice
unless each iteration introduces a materially different consequence.

Emotional variation (confused → understanding → frustrated)
without physical consequence change is insufficient.

evaluations.message: Good action variety. Max repetition: 1.

details.recommendation:
A cause-effect cycle (action → consequence → reset) should not
repeat more than twice unless each iteration introduces a NEW
physical element, obstacle, or escalation.

Example cycle: sharpen → draw → blunt → (reset to sharpen)

Cosmetic variations (stroke pattern, sharpen duration) do not
count as structural escalation.

evaluations.message: No explicit cycles detected.

details.recommendation:
New consequences should be distributed across the timeline,
not clustered at the beginning or end.

No gap longer than 4.5 seconds should pass without a new
visually distinct consequence appearing.

evaluations.message: Good novelty distribution. Max gap: 3.0s.

details.recommendation:
No more than 50% of the video should pass without new
visually distinct physical consequences appearing.

If > 65% of video shows only pattern variations of the same
core action, flag as CRITICAL.

evaluations.message: Good novelty timeline. Static pattern: 0.0%.

details.recommendation:
The final major escalation should not appear after 80% of the video
(12 seconds in a 15-second video) unless the middle contains
strong intermediate escalations.

Late payoffs risk losing viewer attention before the peak.

evaluations.message: Final payoff at 23.0s (88%). Repetitive middle + late payoff risks early exits.

details.recommendation:
The final beat must not be identical or nearly identical
to the opening beat.

A callback is acceptable if it's BIGGER or has a TWIST.
A simple repeat signals lazy structure.

evaluations.message: Final beat repeats opening action without escalation. Payoff must be unique or bigger.

details.recommendation:

Very high complexity typically means 4+ simultaneous high-risk
operations or untested novel requirements.

evaluations.message: Acceptable complexity: low.

details.recommendation:
Before writing a 15-second prompt, verify that the core mechanic
can naturally generate at least 4 visually distinct consequences.

If it cannot, reject the concept.

Do NOT stretch a two-beat teaching contrast into 15 seconds.

details.recommendation:
No single visual state may occupy more than approximately
25–30% of the entire video unless meaningful new physical
consequences occur within that state.

Different dialogue or tiny movements do NOT count
as different visual beats.

details.recommendation:
The same physical action should not repeat more than twice
unless each iteration introduces a materially different consequence.

Emotional variation (confused → understanding → frustrated)
without physical consequence change is insufficient.

passed_rules.message: Good action variety. Max repetition: 1.

details.recommendation:
A cause-effect cycle (action → consequence → reset) should not
repeat more than twice unless each iteration introduces a NEW
physical element, obstacle, or escalation.

Example cycle: sharpen → draw → blunt → (reset to sharpen)

Cosmetic variations (stroke pattern, sharpen duration) do not
count as structural escalation.

passed_rules.message: No explicit cycles detected.

not clustered at the beginning or end.

details.recommendation: Companion to ESCALATION_004 (payoff timing): checks whether attempt-beat intensity rises across the timeline rather than staying flat or declining. details.recommendation: Distinct from ATTEMPT_002 (semantic strategy diversity): ATTEMPT_002 asks whether the character is genuinely trying a different strategy; this asks whether that different strategy will actually LOOK different and be reliably executable by an image-to-video generation model (e.g. Seedance). A deterministic keyword pre-filter flags abstract-intent language ('blocks the escape route', 'tries to outsmart') and vague movement-magnitude phrasing ('slightly moves') on attempt beats, plus a beat-budget estimate (too many attempts for the available duration). An LLM semantic check (check_attempts_are_generation_executable) judges each attempt for a concrete action-result pair and flags attempts that would visually collapse into the same choreography despite different wording. BLOCKER only when NO attempt is judged executable at all or the LLM is unreachable (SERVICE_ERROR); CRITICAL when some attempts are unexecutable or abstract-intent language is matched; WARNING for vague magnitude phrasing or beat-budget pressure alone.

engineInput.prompt:
# Kiko and the Lamp That Hates Being Watched

TYPE: Social Short / Reel
DURATION: 15 seconds
FORMAT: 9:16 vertical, 1080x1920, 24 fps
MODE: Frame to Video, one continuous shot
PRODUCTION MODE: FRESH QUALITY-RESET SHOT

CHARACTER:
Kiko

LOCATION:
Opa’s Tree — learning room / reading corner

LANGUAGE:
Very limited English dialogue.

MANDATORY SPOKEN LINES:
- Kiko: "Hmm?"
- Kiko: "I saw that!"
- Kiko: "Aha!"

CORE IDEA:
Kiko turns on a lamp.
When she looks at it, it behaves normally.
When she looks away, it switches off.
Kiko tests the lamp, thinks she has caught it, but the gag spreads to another light source.

CHARACTER LOCK:
Preserve Kiko exactly:
- dark hair in two buns
- brown eyes
- coral top
- white shorts
- coral shoes
- smart, playful, observant acting

LOCATION LOCK:
Use a cozy treehouse reading corner:
- table or reading chair
- one main lamp
- warm wood textures
- soft books / learning details
- calm interior lighting

LAMP LOCK:
Exactly one main table lamp or reading lamp.
It does not move.
It does not talk.
Its trick is only this:
when watched, it behaves;
when unwatched, it switches off or on at the wrong time.

CAMERA:
Locked medium-wide vertical framing.
Keep Kiko and lamp visible together.

MANDATORY SPOKEN DIALOGUE / LIP-SYNC LOCK:
Speech is REQUIRED.
Kiko must audibly say:
1. "Hmm?" around 01.0s
2. "I saw that!" around 07.0s
3. "Aha!" around 10.5s

ACTION TIMING:
00.0–02.0s
Kiko switches on the lamp and starts to read or look at the table.
She turns her head away for a moment.
The lamp switches off.
Kiko turns back and says: "Hmm?"

02.0–05.0s
Kiko switches it on again and stares at it.
It stays on.
She slowly looks away.
It switches off again.

05.0–08.0s
Kiko quickly spins back and points at it.
She says: "I saw that!"

08.0–11.5s
Kiko gets clever.
She uses a small mirror or reflective object to “watch” the lamp indirectly.
The lamp stays on.
Kiko smiles proudly and says: "Aha!"

11.5–13.5s
Just as Kiko celebrates, a second small light in the room flickers on or off instead.
Kiko looks toward it, surprised.

13.5–15.0s
When Kiko looks back at the main lamp, it is off again.
She lunges back toward it, matching the opening rhythm for loop.

SOUND:
Soft room ambience, light click sounds, tiny electric switch sounds.
No scary sound design.
Dialogue must be clearly audible.

AVOID:
horror lamp, flickering horror room, monster light, darkness scare, extra characters, crying, subtitles, logo, watermark, cuts, zoom.

details.recommendation:
Before writing a 15-second prompt, verify that the core mechanic
can naturally generate at least 4 visually distinct consequences.

If it cannot, reject the concept.

Do NOT stretch a two-beat teaching contrast into 15 seconds.

evaluations.message: Sufficient consequence variety: 6 distinct consequences.

details.recommendation:
No single visual state may occupy more than approximately
25–30% of the entire video unless meaningful new physical
consequences occur within that state.

Different dialogue or tiny movements do NOT count
as different visual beats.

evaluations.message: Good visual state distribution. Max state: 23.3%.

details.recommendation:
The same physical action should not repeat more than twice
unless each iteration introduces a materially different consequence.

Emotional variation (confused → understanding → frustrated)
without physical consequence change is insufficient.

evaluations.message: Good action variety. Max repetition: 1.

details.recommendation:
A cause-effect cycle (action → consequence → reset) should not
repeat more than twice unless each iteration introduces a NEW
physical element, obstacle, or escalation.

Example cycle: sharpen → draw → blunt → (reset to sharpen)

Cosmetic variations (stroke pattern, sharpen duration) do not
count as structural escalation.

evaluations.message: No explicit cycles detected.

details.recommendation:
New consequences should be distributed across the timeline,
not clustered at the beginning or end.

No gap longer than 4.5 seconds should pass without a new
visually distinct consequence appearing.

evaluations.message: Good novelty distribution. Max gap: 3.5s.

details.recommendation:
No more than 50% of the video should pass without new
visually distinct physical consequences appearing.

If > 65% of video shows only pattern variations of the same
core action, flag as CRITICAL.

evaluations.message: Good novelty timeline. Static pattern: 0.0%.

details.recommendation:
The final major escalation should not appear after 80% of the video
(12 seconds in a 15-second video) unless the middle contains
strong intermediate escalations.

Late payoffs risk losing viewer attention before the peak.

evaluations.message: Final payoff at 13.5s. Late but middle is strong.

details.recommendation:
The final beat must not be identical or nearly identical
to the opening beat.

A callback is acceptable if it's BIGGER or has a TWIST.
A simple repeat signals lazy structure.

evaluations.message: Final payoff is distinct from opening.

details.recommendation:

details.recommendation:

repeat more than twice unless each iteration introduces a NEW
physical element, obstacle, or escalation.

count as structural escalation.

details.recommendation: Distinct from ATTEMPT_002 (semantic strategy diversity): ATTEMPT_002 asks whether the character is genuinely trying a different strategy; this asks whether that different strategy will actually LOOK different and be reliably executable by an image-to-video generation model (e.g. Seedance). A deterministic keyword pre-filter flags abstract-intent language ('blocks the escape route', 'tries to outsmart') and vague movement-magnitude phrasing ('slightly moves') on attempt beats, plus a beat-budget estimate (too many attempts for the available duration). An LLM semantic check (check_attempts_are_generation_executable) judges each attempt for a concrete action-result pair and flags attempts that would visually collapse into the same choreography despite different wording. engineInput.prompt:
# Mimi and the Snack Box That Keeps Changing

TYPE: Social Short / Reel
DURATION: 15 seconds
FORMAT: 9:16 vertical, 1080x1920, 24 fps
MODE: Frame to Video, one continuous shot
PRODUCTION MODE: FRESH QUALITY-RESET SHOT

CHARACTER:
Mimi

LOCATION:
Pompom Hills — picnic table / snack table area

LANGUAGE:
Very limited English dialogue.

MANDATORY SPOKEN LINES:
- Mimi: "Snack time!"
- Mimi: "What?"
- Mimi: "There!"

CORE IDEA:
Mimi wants a cracker from a snack box, but every time she opens it, something different is inside.
She tests the box again and again, then thinks she has solved it.
At the very end, the box still wins.

CHARACTER LOCK:
Preserve Mimi exactly:
- pastel-blue bunny
- white belly / muzzle
- long floppy ears
- green eyes
- pink nose
- yellow shirt
- soft rounded Pompom Hills design

LOCATION LOCK:
Use a simple cute snack setup:
- low table
- cheerful background
- a few picnic or snack details
- bright daylight
- clean readable space

BOX LOCK:
Exactly one snack box with a lid.
The box stays in the same place.
It never grows, moves away, or becomes scary.
Its only trick is that contents change between openings.

CAMERA:
Locked medium-wide vertical composition.
Keep visible:
- Mimi full or near full body
- full snack box
- tabletop

MANDATORY SPOKEN DIALOGUE / LIP-SYNC LOCK:
Speech is REQUIRED.
Mimi must audibly say:
1. "Snack time!" around 00.5s
2. "What?" around 04.5s
3. "There!" around 10.5s

ACTION TIMING:
00.0–02.0s
Mimi happily reaches for the box and opens it.
She expects a cracker.
Inside is an apple instead.
Mimi says: "Snack time!"

02.0–05.0s
Mimi closes and reopens the box.
Now there is a banana or spoon inside.
Mimi blinks and says: "What?"

05.0–08.0s
Mimi closes and opens it again.
Now a silly wrong item appears, like a sock or block.
Mimi becomes determined.

08.0–11.5s
Mimi turns the box slightly, taps it, closes it carefully, then opens it.
Finally, the cracker appears.
Mimi points proudly and says: "There!"

11.5–13.5s
Mimi reaches in to grab the cracker.
The lid suddenly flips shut or the cracker pops back down out of reach.

13.5–15.0s
Mimi reopens the box and sees another wrong item again.
She reacts and immediately leans in for another try, matching the opening rhythm for loop.

SOUND:
Small lid open/close sounds, light table taps, cute object swap sounds.
No heavy music.
Dialogue must be clear.

AVOID:
extra characters, spooky magic, talking box, scary object changes, crying, long final hold, text, subtitles, logo, watermark, cuts, zoom.

# Mimi vs. the Sneaky Door — Compact Generation Card

## Final Target

- 15 seconds total: 3 × 5-second clips
- 1080×1920, 9:16 vertical, 24 fps
- Location: canonical Kiko's Home front porch
- Style: warm, rounded, matte Pompom Hills preschool animation
- Language: English only
- OpenArt music: OFF

## Attachments

- Mimi: `01-CHARACTERS/drawings/mimi.png`
- Kiko: `01-CHARACTERS/drawings/kiko.png`
- World: `POMPOM_HILLS_PRODUCTION/02_WORLDS/KIKOS_HOME/01_HERO_VIEW/hero-view.png`
- Separate Negative Prompt: `mimi-sneaky-door-negative-prompt.txt`

## Render Order

### 1. Build `@image1`

Use `start-and-loop-frame-prompts.md`. Approve Mimi identity, vertical door staging, safe movement space and exact Kiko's Home identity.

### 2. Render Shot 01

Use `mimi-sneaky-door-shot-01-openart.md` with `@image1`.

Action: door closes → Mimi “Huh?” → strong pull → smaller tug → puzzled stable end.

Export the unmodified final frame as `@image2`. Reject it if Mimi, door, world, colour or camera drifted.

### 3. Render Shot 02

Use `mimi-sneaky-door-shot-02-openart.md` with `@image2`.

Action: two real steps away → door opens once → Mimi turns → door closes once → clever realization.

Export the unmodified final frame as `@image3`. Reject it if the chain degraded.

### 4. Build Optional `@image4`

Use the loop-wipe section in `start-and-loop-frame-prompts.md`. It must match the exact door material and warm exposure.

### 5. Render Shot 03

Use `mimi-sneaky-door-shot-03-openart.md` with `@image3`; add `@image4` as final-frame anchor if supported.

Action: two fake steps → spring-back and “Got you!” → Kiko visible doorway entrance and “Surprise!” → controlled door-to-lens wipe.

### 6. Assemble

engineInput.prompt:
# Kiko vs Spot-Stealing Cat — OpenArt / Seedance 2.0 Mini

## Core concept
Kiko wants to sit down.

**Single animal rule:** whenever Kiko truly commits to sitting in an empty spot, the cat claims that exact spot first.

## Prompt
Colorful high-quality stylized 3D preschool animation in the official Pompom Hills style. 9:16 vertical, 15 seconds, one continuous fixed-camera shot in a simple cozy room with three clearly readable open sitting spots on the floor/low seating area. Keep geometry simple and uncluttered. No cuts, no zoom, no shake.

Use the official Kiko design exactly: brown hair in two buns, large brown eyes, coral/pink long-sleeve top, white shorts, pink shoes. Use one cute stylized cat only, smooth low-detail coat, calm expression.

### Frame zero — conflict already happening
Start with Kiko already lowering herself toward an empty spot. At the same moment, the cat is curling into that exact spot just before Kiko sits. Kiko is visibly caught mid-squat.

### Attempt 1 — switch spot
Kiko immediately changes to a second nearby sitting spot. As soon as she clearly commits downward, the cat makes one short move and settles into that second spot first. Kiko stops safely and gives a suspicious side-eye.

### Attempt 2 — opposite spot
Kiko walks to a third open spot on the other side. She checks the cat, then starts to sit. The cat calmly reaches the target first and curls up. Kiko straightens and gives a tiny determined nod.

### Attempt 3 — decoy
Kiko pretends to sit in one spot, then quickly changes direction and commits to another. The cat ignores the fake and claims Kiko's real target spot just before she sits.

### Fake win + final payoff
The cat is looking away. Kiko slowly approaches the last empty spot. The cat does not move. Kiko gives a tiny proud smile and begins lowering herself. At the exact moment she truly commits, the cat makes one final short move into the spot and curls up. Kiko freezes in a squat just above the floor. She looks down. Cat looks up, perfectly comfortable. Hard cut.

## Performance
Kiko stays curious, kind, determined and slightly serious. Cat is never aggressive or smug; simply calm and certain.

## Guardrails
- one Kiko only
- one cat only
- no pillows or extra active props
- same rule throughout: SIT COMMITMENT -> CAT CLAIMS TARGET
- no Kiko-cat contact
- no falling
- no jumping cat
- no running
- simple short cat repositioning only
- fixed camera
- one continuous take
- hard cut on Kiko's suspended squat

engineInput.prompt:
Create a highly engaging 15-second vertical 9:16 Pompom Hills short.

USE THE OFFICIAL EXISTING LUCA CHARACTER REFERENCE EXACTLY.
Do not redesign Luca.

PHYSICAL RULE
STICKY — the red ball sticks to surfaces instead of bouncing.

SETTING
Simple sunny Pompom Hills garden.
One wooden play wall, green grass, minimal background.

MAIN OBJECT
One bright red soft rubber ball.

CAMERA
Single continuous visual flow.
Medium shot with Luca and the wall both clearly visible.
No establishing shot.

0.0–0.8 SEC — HARD HOOK
FIRST FRAME:
Luca has JUST thrown the red ball at the wooden wall.
Instead of bouncing back, the ball is already STUCK flat to the wall.
Luca is frozen with both hands half-raised, eyes wide.
The impossible sticky ball must dominate the opening.

SFX: THWIP — STICK.

0.8–3.0 SEC — REACTION
Luca walks straight to the ball and pulls it with one hand.
It will not move.
He uses both hands.

3.0–6.0 SEC — FIRST ATTEMPT
Luca pulls harder.
The ball stretches toward him like soft chewing gum while its center remains stuck to the wall.
He lets go.

SNAP!
The ball instantly returns to the wall.

6.0–9.0 SEC — ESCALATION
Luca grabs the ball again with both hands and leans backward.
This time the BALL stays stuck and the WOODEN WALL itself flexes slightly toward Luca like soft rubber.
Luca’s eyes widen.
He immediately releases it.

BOING!
The wall returns safely to normal.

9.0–12.0 SEC — SECOND ATTEMPT
The ball finally drops from the wall by itself.
Luca catches it.
He squeezes it gently.
It behaves like a normal ball.
He smiles.

12.0–14.0 SEC — FAKE RESOLUTION
Luca carefully tosses the ball once between his hands.
Normal.
He relaxes.

14.0–15.0 SEC — FINAL TWIST
Luca gives the ball one tiny playful toss upward.
It drops directly onto his CHEEK and sticks there with a soft PLUP.
Luca goes cross-eyed trying to look at it.

PLUP! — HARD CUT.

SAFETY
The ball is soft.
It sticks to Luca’s cheek only, never covering his nose or mouth.

DIALOGUE
None.

NO narrator.
NO text overlay.
NO logo.
NO watermark.

details.recommendation:
Before writing a 15-second prompt, verify that the core mechanic
can naturally generate at least 4 visually distinct consequences.

If it cannot, reject the concept.

Do NOT stretch a two-beat teaching contrast into 15 seconds.

evaluations.message: Sufficient consequence variety: 7 distinct consequences.

details.recommendation:
No single visual state may occupy more than approximately
25–30% of the entire video unless meaningful new physical
consequences occur within that state.

Different dialogue or tiny movements do NOT count
as different visual beats.

evaluations.message: Good visual state distribution. Max state: 20.0%.

details.recommendation:
The same physical action should not repeat more than twice
unless each iteration introduces a materially different consequence.

Emotional variation (confused → understanding → frustrated)
without physical consequence change is insufficient.

evaluations.message: Good action variety. Max repetition: 1.

details.recommendation:
A cause-effect cycle (action → consequence → reset) should not
repeat more than twice unless each iteration introduces a NEW
physical element, obstacle, or escalation.

Example cycle: sharpen → draw → blunt → (reset to sharpen)

Cosmetic variations (stroke pattern, sharpen duration) do not
count as structural escalation.

evaluations.message: No explicit cycles detected.

details.recommendation:
New consequences should be distributed across the timeline,
not clustered at the beginning or end.

No gap longer than 4.5 seconds should pass without a new
visually distinct consequence appearing.

evaluations.message: Good novelty distribution. Max gap: 3.0s.

details.recommendation:
No more than 50% of the video should pass without new
visually distinct physical consequences appearing.

If > 65% of video shows only pattern variations of the same
core action, flag as CRITICAL.

evaluations.message: Good novelty timeline. Static pattern: 0.0%.

details.recommendation:
The final major escalation should not appear after 80% of the video
(12 seconds in a 15-second video) unless the middle contains
strong intermediate escalations.

Late payoffs risk losing viewer attention before the peak.

evaluations.message: Final payoff at 14.0s. Late but middle is strong.

details.recommendation:
The final beat must not be identical or nearly identical
to the opening beat.

A callback is acceptable if it's BIGGER or has a TWIST.
A simple repeat signals lazy structure.

evaluations.message: Final payoff is distinct from opening.

details.recommendation:
Prompts marked as "very_high" complexity should not proceed
to render without human review and risk acceptance.

Very high complexity typically means 4+ simultaneous high-risk
operations or untested novel requirements.

evaluations.message: Overall complexity: high. Render uncertain. Consider simplifications.

engineInput.prompt:
Create a highly engaging 15–18 second vertical 9:16 Pompom Hills Instagram Reel.

Use the official existing Pompom Hills character references exactly.
MAIN CHARACTER: KIKO

Do not redesign Kiko.
Do not replace her with a generic child.

SERIES:
Pompom English — What’s Wrong?

CORE ENGLISH:
CHAIR
UP
DOWN
“It’s upside down!”

SETTING:
Bright Pompom Hills playroom or garden patio.
Keep the environment simple and instantly readable.

--------------------------------------------------
0.0–0.8 SEC — HARD SCROLL-STOP HOOK
--------------------------------------------------

Start immediately.

Kiko runs toward a chair to sit down.

BUT THE CHAIR IS COMPLETELY UPSIDE DOWN.

Legs pointing into the air.

Kiko is already halfway into the sitting motion before noticing.

She freezes inches above it.

Eyes huge.

She blurts:

“WHAT?!”

NO establishing shot.
The upside-down chair must dominate the first frame.

--------------------------------------------------
0.8–3.5 SEC
--------------------------------------------------

Kiko points:

“A CHAIR!”

Then looks confused.

She says clearly:

“It’s upside down!”

She grabs the chair and flips it correctly.

--------------------------------------------------
3.5–6.0 SEC
--------------------------------------------------

Kiko smiles proudly.

“Up… down!”

She points upward while saying UP.
Then downward while saying DOWN.

She turns around to sit.

--------------------------------------------------
6.0–8.5 SEC — FIRST ESCALATION
--------------------------------------------------

The instant Kiko turns away—

FLIP!

The chair turns upside down by itself.

Kiko sits toward empty space and catches herself at the last second.

She spins around.

--------------------------------------------------
8.5–11.5 SEC
--------------------------------------------------

Kiko flips it back.

She stares directly at the chair.

Chair stays normal.

Kiko slowly turns her head away.

FLIP!

She immediately looks back.

Chair is upside down.

--------------------------------------------------
11.5–14.5 SEC — COMEDY PAYOFF
--------------------------------------------------

Kiko becomes determined.

She keeps staring at the chair.

She slowly walks backward toward it without looking away.

She says:

“Stay DOWN!”

The chair behaves.

Kiko smiles.

--------------------------------------------------
14.5–17.0 SEC — TWIST + LOOP
--------------------------------------------------

Kiko finally sits.

The ENTIRE chair suddenly flips upside down WITH Kiko on it.

Kiko ends upside down and shouts:

“AGAIN?!”

Cut immediately.

Loop back to the first upside-down chair.

--------------------------------------------------
MANDATORY SPOKEN DIALOGUE / LIP-SYNC LOCK
--------------------------------------------------

Exact English dialogue REQUIRED:

Kiko:
“WHAT?!”

Kiko:
“A CHAIR!”

Kiko:
“It’s upside down!”

Kiko:
“Up… down!”

Kiko:
“Stay DOWN!”

Kiko:
“AGAIN?!”

All lines must be clearly audible English.

Visible mouth movement.
Accurate lip-sync.

Do not:
- remove dialogue
- translate it
- replace dialogue with subtitles
- create a silent version
- add narration

--------------------------------------------------
INSTAGRAM RETENTION RULES
--------------------------------------------------

Something must change every 1–2 seconds.

The problem must be understandable without sound.

Do not make the chair movement subtle.

Chair flips must be fast and visually obvious.

No moral lesson.
No slow ending.
No waiting after final joke.
No text generated inside scene.
